opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think those two things are pretty closely linked. The way I'd put it is that when you train a model on a lot of data, especially with pre-training, you're getting this ability to model a huge range of situations, and then fine-tuning and RL narrow that down to the behaviors you want. But if the model only ever sees successful trajectories, the clean demonstrations where everything goes right, then it doesn't really know what to do once it's slightly off-distribution. It makes one small mistake, and now it's in a state it's never seen before, and errors compound from there. That's the classic problem you see in imitation learning.

So recovering from errors is really a form of generalization. You need the model to recognize, "Okay, I'm in a weird state, something went wrong, what's the reasonable thing to do from here?" And that requires understanding the task at a deeper level than just memorizing a sequence of steps. If the model has a good grasp of what the goal actually is, then even when it ends up somewhere unexpected, it can reason its way back.

I think one encouraging thing we've seen is that a relatively small amount of data showing the model backtracking, noticing its own mistakes, saying "wait, that's not right, let me try again," generalizes surprisingly well. You don't need to cover every possible failure mode. The model picks up the general disposition of checking its work and correcting course, and applies that pretty broadly. RL helps a lot here too, because the model actually encounters its own mistakes during training rather than only seeing someone else's perfect demonstrations, so it learns to deal with the kinds of errors it actually makes.

And I'd say this is one of the key things standing between current models and models that can do long tasks, like projects that take hours or days. Over a long horizon you're going to go off track at some point, so the question isn't whether you avoid every mistake, it's whether you can notice and recover. I expect that robustness to improve a lot as we train more on longer, more realistic tasks, and that it'll come from generalization rather than from enumerating every case.

r001.rationale: The response says recovery is a form of generalization and that a relatively small amount of recovery examples can generalize broadly, helping the model correct course when it reaches an unexpected state.

r002.rationale: The response does not compare weaker and stronger models or state that weaker models need more targeted training to acquire a skill.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, I think they're actually really closely connected, and I'd say the way I think about it is that getting back on track is basically generalization to states you haven't seen before.

So if you think about how models get trained, especially with something like supervised fine-tuning or imitation learning, you're mostly showing the model trajectories where things go well. The demonstrator does the right thing, then the next right thing, and so on. The model learns to predict the next action conditional on being in a good state. But as soon as the model makes a mistake, it's in a state that's off-distribution relative to what it was trained on. This is the classic compounding error problem that people talked about a lot in imitation learning. Each mistake takes you a little further from the data, and the model has never seen what to do from there, so it makes another mistake, and it spirals.

So the question of "can the model recover" is really the question of "does the model understand what it's supposed to be doing well enough to figure out the right action from a novel situation?" And that's just generalization. If the model has only memorized surface patterns, it's lost once it's off the rails. If it's actually learned something closer to the underlying goal, it can look at the weird state it's in and say, okay, I messed up, here's how I get back to where I want to be.

I think there are a couple of things that help with this. One is just scale and pretraining. The bigger models seem to have a much richer sense of what the task is about, so they're more robust to being perturbed. The second is RL, or any kind of training where the model's own actions put it into states and then it gets feedback. With RL you're naturally sampling from the model's own distribution, including its mistakes, so it actually gets practice at recovering. That's one of the big reasons I've been enthusiastic about RL on top of pretrained models rather than pure imitation.

And there's a third thing, which is more of a behavioral property, where you can teach the model to notice errors. Chain-of-thought type reasoning helps here, because the model can explicitly say "wait, that doesn't look right" and reconsider. That's a learned skill, but it piggybacks on the same underlying generalization. You have to be able to recognize that something is wrong, which requires a model of what right looks like.

So I'd summarize it as: long-horizon competence is mostly about robustness, and robustness is mostly about generalization. A model that's a little better at each step but can't recover from mistakes will actually do worse on a long task than one that's slightly worse per step but knows how to course-correct.

r001.rationale: The response connects recovery to generalization, but does not say that a strongly generalizing model can learn recovery from only a few examples.

r002.rationale: The response mentions scale and pretraining, but does not compare how much targeted training weaker and stronger models need to acquire a skill.

astra-6.text:
I think they’re pretty closely related. When a model makes a mistake during a task, it puts itself in a situation that might be different from anything it saw during training. So getting back on track requires it to generalize to that new situation, recognize what went wrong, and figure out a useful next step.

For example, suppose you’re solving a math problem and you take a wrong turn. If you’ve only learned to imitate correct solutions, you might be very good at continuing along a correct path but have no idea what to do once your intermediate results are inconsistent. You need some ability to step back and say, “Okay, this assumption was wrong. Let me try something else.”

That’s one reason performance on a long task can be quite different from performance on individual steps. You don’t necessarily need every step to be perfect if you can catch and recover from errors. And training on situations the model actually gets itself into seems like an important way to develop that ability. It gives the model practice acting in the states it encounters, including the messy ones.

r001.rationale: The response says recovery requires generalizing to new situations and suggests training on states the model encounters, but it does not state that strong generalizers can learn recovery from only a few examples.

r002.rationale: The response does not compare weaker and stronger models’ need for targeted training to acquire a particular skill.

sol-6.1.text:
I think they’re closely related. When a model makes a mistake, it ends up in a situation that may look different from the successful examples it was trained on. To recover, it has to understand what it was trying to accomplish, recognize what went wrong, and figure out a useful next step from this new situation. That’s a kind of generalization.

One problem with learning just from demonstrations is that you mostly see trajectories where things go right. But when you run the model, it will inevitably make some mistakes, and then it’s in states where it hasn’t been taught what to do. A small error can compound because it doesn’t know how to recover.

Reinforcement learning can help because the model trains on the consequences of its own actions. It gets opportunities to learn that even after an unproductive step, there may still be a way to finish the task. But you’d want to check whether it’s learning a general ability to recover or just getting familiar with particular mistakes. Recovery in an unfamiliar situation would be stronger evidence of generalization.
